learningObjectives.title: The Civil Rights movement and the Troubles
Direct rule and attempts at a solution
The path to the Good Friday Agreement 1998

questions.q: In which year was the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) founded?
questions.explain: NICRA was formed in 1967 to campaign against discrimination faced by the Catholic/nationalist community.

questions.q: Which slogan summed up the civil rights demand for reform of local council elections?
options: 'No surrender'
'One man, one vote'
'Ulster says no'
'Brits out'
questions.explain: Campaigners demanded 'one man, one vote' to end the system where only ratepayers could vote and some business owners had extra votes in local elections.

questions.q: Why was gerrymandering a major civil rights grievance?
options: It banned Catholics from voting in general elections
It redrew electoral boundaries so unionists controlled councils despite nationalist majorities
It forced Catholics to pay higher taxes
It gave the Republic control of local councils
questions.explain: Gerrymandering rigged ward boundaries so that unionists could win control of councils even in areas with nationalist population majorities, such as Derry.

questions.q: What happened at the civil rights march in Derry on 5 October 1968?
options: The march passed off peacefully
The RUC baton-charged marchers in scenes shown on television
The British army opened fire on the crowd
The march was cancelled by NICRA
questions.explain: The RUC's baton charge on 5 October 1968 was filmed and broadcast worldwide, drawing international attention to the civil rights campaign.

questions.q: Why was the People's Democracy march attacked at Burntollet Bridge in January 1969 significant?
options: It ended all civil rights protest in Northern Ireland
It increased nationalist anger and distrust of the RUC, raising tensions
It led directly to the Good Friday Agreement
It persuaded the government to abolish Stormont
questions.explain: The ambush of the Belfast-to-Derry march by loyalists, with the RUC seen to do little to protect marchers, deepened nationalist distrust and heightened sectarian tension.

questions.q: In August 1969 the British government responded to escalating violence such as the Battle of the Bogside by taking which action?
options: Introducing internment without trial
Deploying British army troops onto the streets of Northern Ireland
Suspending the Stormont parliament
Signing the Sunningdale Agreement
questions.explain: British troops were sent in during August 1969 (Operation Banner) as violence overwhelmed the RUC.

questions.q: Why did many Catholics initially welcome the arrival of British troops in 1969?
options: The troops promised a united Ireland
They saw the army as protection against loyalist attacks and the RUC/B-Specials
The troops handed control to the Irish government
The soldiers were mostly local Catholics
questions.explain: Many Catholics first regarded the soldiers as neutral protectors against loyalist mobs and a hostile police force, though this goodwill soon broke down.

questions.q: A historian argues that a 1971 government policy backfired by driving Catholics towards the IRA. Which policy is being described?
options: The introduction of internment without trial
The abolition of the B-Specials
The signing of the Anglo-Irish Agreement
The imposition of direct rule
questions.explain: Internment (August 1971) targeted mainly nationalists, was applied unjustly and boosted support for the Provisional IRA rather than reducing violence.

questions.q: What occurred on Bloody Sunday, 30 January 1972, in Derry?
options: The IRA bombed the city centre killing dozens
British Parachute Regiment soldiers shot dead 13 unarmed civil rights marchers
Loyalist paramilitaries attacked a Catholic estate
The RUC clashed with soldiers over policing
questions.explain: On Bloody Sunday, soldiers of the Parachute Regiment opened fire on an anti-internment march, killing 13 people on the day (a 14th died later).

questions.q: What was a major consequence of Bloody Sunday?
options: The IRA immediately declared a ceasefire
Nationalist anger surged and IRA recruitment increased sharply
Stormont was strengthened
The civil rights movement achieved all its demands
questions.explain: Bloody Sunday alienated the nationalist community from the state and became a powerful recruiting boost for the Provisional IRA.

questions.q: What did the British government do in March 1972?
options: Introduced the Anglo-Irish Agreement
Suspended the Stormont parliament and imposed direct rule from London
Signed the Good Friday Agreement
Abolished the RUC
questions.explain: In March 1972 Stormont was prorogued and Northern Ireland was governed directly from Westminster, with William Whitelaw as the first Secretary of State.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the 1973 Sunningdale Agreement?
options: To create a power-sharing Executive and a Council of Ireland
To introduce internment
To withdraw all British troops
To hold a referendum on a united Ireland
questions.explain: Sunningdale set up a power-sharing Executive of unionists and nationalists plus a Council of Ireland linking North and South.

questions.q: Why did many unionists strongly oppose the Sunningdale Agreement?
options: It abolished the Orange Order
They feared the Council of Ireland would lead to a united Ireland
It banned Protestant marches
It gave too much power to the British army
questions.explain: Unionists saw the proposed Council of Ireland as a step towards Irish unity, fuelling fierce opposition to power-sharing.

questions.q: In 1974 the power-sharing Executive collapsed. Which action was most responsible for bringing it down?
options: An IRA bombing campaign in England
The Ulster Workers' Council strike that shut down power and services
A British army mutiny
A vote in the Dublin parliament
questions.explain: The loyalist UWC general strike in May 1974 paralysed Northern Ireland by cutting electricity and essential services, forcing the Executive to collapse.

questions.q: Who was the first republican hunger striker to die in the Maze prison in 1981?
options: Gerry Adams
Bobby Sands
Martin McGuinness
John Hume
questions.explain: Bobby Sands died in May 1981 after 66 days on hunger strike, the first of ten republican prisoners to die during the protest.

questions.q: Why was Bobby Sands's election as an MP during the 1981 hunger strike politically significant?
options: It proved the hunger strike had failed
It showed republicans could win electoral support, encouraging Sinn Fein's political strategy
It led to the immediate release of all prisoners
It ended direct rule
questions.explain: Sands's by-election victory demonstrated the electoral appeal of republicanism and helped push Sinn Fein towards a combined political and paramilitary ('ballot box and Armalite') approach.

questions.q: The 1985 Anglo-Irish Agreement was signed by Margaret Thatcher and which Irish leader?
options: Albert Reynolds
Garret FitzGerald
Bertie Ahern
Charles Haughey
questions.explain: The Anglo-Irish Agreement was signed in 1985 by British PM Margaret Thatcher and Irish Taoiseach Garret FitzGerald.

questions.q: A photograph shows unionists in 1985 holding banners reading 'Ulster Says No'. What were they protesting against?
options: The Good Friday Agreement
The Anglo-Irish Agreement giving the Republic a consultative role
The introduction of internment
The Sunningdale Agreement
questions.explain: 'Ulster Says No' was the unionist campaign against the Anglo-Irish Agreement, which for the first time gave the Irish government a formal say in Northern Ireland's affairs.

questions.q: The 1993 Downing Street Declaration was issued by British PM John Major and which Irish Taoiseach?
options: Garret FitzGerald
Albert Reynolds
Bertie Ahern
Jack Lynch
questions.explain: The Downing Street Declaration was made jointly by John Major and Albert Reynolds, helping to open the way to paramilitary ceasefires.

questions.q: Why were the 1994 paramilitary ceasefires important for the peace process?
options: They ended direct rule immediately
They created conditions allowing inclusive political talks to begin
They dissolved the IRA and UVF permanently
They united Ireland
questions.explain: The IRA and loyalist ceasefires of 1994 reduced violence and made it possible to bring parties, including Sinn Fein, into negotiations.

questions.q: Who chaired the multi-party talks that led to the Good Friday Agreement?
options: Bill Clinton
US Senator George Mitchell
Tony Blair
Bertie Ahern
questions.explain: American senator George Mitchell chaired the negotiations and set out principles of non-violence for participation in the talks.

questions.q: On what date was the Good Friday Agreement reached in 1998?
options: 10 April 1998
15 August 1998
31 August 1994
questions.explain: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was concluded on 10 April 1998 and later endorsed by referendum on 22 May 1998.

questions.q: What did the 'principle of consent' in the Good Friday Agreement establish?
options: That the IRA must decommission first
That Northern Ireland's status would change only if a majority of its people voted for it
That the Republic would govern the North
That direct rule would continue forever
questions.explain: The consent principle stated that any change to Northern Ireland's constitutional position required the agreement of a majority of its population.

questions.q: A student needs an example showing that peace remained fragile even after the 1998 Agreement. Which event best supports this?
options: The Omagh bombing carried out by the Real IRA in August 1998
The signing of the Sunningdale Agreement
The 1981 hunger strikes
The introduction of direct rule in 1972
questions.explain: The Omagh bombing, the single worst atrocity of the Troubles, showed that dissident republicans opposed to the Agreement could still threaten the peace.

specSource: CCEA GCSE History (2017) specification; Changing Relations: Northern Ireland & its Neighbours 1965-98
